title: Licensing Conditions
description: Understanding UK amateur radio licence tiers, Ofcom regulations, callsigns, permitted bands, power limits, and operating conditions.
content:
UK Amateur Radio Licensing

Amateur radio in the United Kingdom is regulated by Ofcom (the Office of Communications) (Ofcom, 2024). To transmit on amateur radio frequencies, you must hold a valid amateur radio licence. The licence exists for the purpose of self-training in radio communications (Betts, 2019) — it is a leisure activity and must not be used for commercial purposes.

Three Licence Tiers

Licence LevelCallsign PrefixMax PowerEquipment
FoundationM3 (legacy) / M6 (new)10 WattsCommercial or commercially-supplied kit only — no home design
Intermediate2E0 / 2E150 WattsMay build from published designs or magazine articles
FullM0 / M1 (legacy: G)400 WattsFull freedom to design, build and modify

Callsign Structure

Your callsign is your unique identifier on the air. A UK Foundation callsign follows the format M6 + three letters (e.g., M6ABC). The legacy prefix M3 is no longer issued for new licences. You may choose your last 3 letters from available combinations when applying.

Regional Secondary Locators

When operating from different parts of the UK, a letter is inserted after the prefix number:

  • W — Wales (e.g., MW6ABC)
  • M — Scotland (e.g., MM6ABC)
  • I — Northern Ireland (e.g., MI6ABC)
  • D — Isle of Man
  • J — Jersey
  • U — Guernsey
  • No locator — England

Callsign Suffixes

  • /M — Mobile (vehicle, pedestrian, or inland waterway boat)
  • /A — Alternate address (building with different postal address from licence address)
  • /P — Portable (fixed location without a postal address)

Licence Conditions

  • Station identification: As frequently as practicable; traditionally at least every 15 minutes
  • Messages: Only to other UK licensed amateurs
  • Encryption: Not permitted
  • Broadcasting: Not permitted (CQ calls excepted)
  • Unattended transmission: Not permitted at Foundation level
  • Supervised operation: Another UK licensed amateur may operate under your direct supervision using your callsign
  • Change of address: Must notify Ofcom immediately
  • Ofcom inspection: Must permit access at any reasonable time; Ofcom may require modification or shutdown
  • Overseas use: Foundation licence is NOT recognised internationally — do not operate abroad

Applying for Your Licence

  • Online: Free — log on to Ofcom licensing system using result letter details
  • Postal: £20 fee (waived if 75 or over)
  • Renewal: Log on every 5 years minimum to confirm details

The Exam

The Foundation exam consists of 26 multiple-choice questions (4 options each), with a 55-minute time limit. You need 19 correct answers (73%) to pass (Betts, 2019). A band plan, frequency/wavelength chart, and licence schedule Table A are provided during the exam.

Study Tips

For the exam, make sure you know: the three licence levels and their power limits, the Foundation callsign format (M6 + 3 letters), that Ofcom is the regulator, the requirement to identify your station, the key operating conditions, and that the Foundation licence is NOT valid overseas.

References

  • Betts, A. (2019) Foundation Licence Now! 5th edn. Bedford: RSGB, pp. 1–26.
  • Ofcom (2024) Amateur Radio Licence Terms, Conditions and Limitations. Available at: https://www.ofcom.org.uk/manage-your-licence/radiocommunication-licences/amateur-radio (Accessed: 15 March 2026).
  • RSGB (2024) Foundation Exam Syllabus. Available at: https://rsgb.org/main/clubs-and-education/for-students/ (Accessed: 15 March 2026).

title: Technical Basics
description: Fundamental electronics: voltage, current, resistance, Ohm's Law, power, AC/DC, frequency, wavelength, decibels, and components.
content:
Electricity Fundamentals

Understanding basic electrical concepts is essential for amateur radio. There are three fundamental quantities:

SymbolQuantityUnit
VPotential Difference / VoltageVolt (V)
ICurrentAmpere (A)
RResistanceOhm (Ω)
PPowerWatt (W)
fFrequencyHertz (Hz)
λWavelengthMetre (m)

Metric Prefixes

PrefixSymbolMultiplierExample
millim× 0.0015mA = 0.005A
kilok× 1,0002.3kV = 2300V
MegaM× 1,000,0004MHz = 4,000,000Hz

Ohm's Law

Ohm's Law describes the relationship between voltage, current, and resistance:

  • V = I × R (Voltage = Current × Resistance)
  • I = V / R (Current = Voltage ÷ Resistance)
  • R = V / I (Resistance = Voltage ÷ Current)

Power Formulae

  • P = V × I
  • P = I² × R
  • P = V² / R

Worked examples from the book:

  • 3V bulb at 0.3A: P = 3 × 0.3 = 0.9W
  • 230V fire at 10A: P = 230 × 10 = 2300W (2.3kW)
  • 10Ω bulb at 3V: I = 3/10 = 0.3A

Series and Parallel Circuits

Resistors

  • Series: R = R1 + R2 + R3
  • Parallel: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3

Capacitors (opposite to resistors)

  • Series: 1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2
  • Parallel: C = C1 + C2 + C3

Inductors (same as resistors)

  • Series: L = L1 + L2
  • Parallel: 1/L = 1/L1 + 1/L2

Components

  • Resistor (Ω) — Limits current flow. Higher value = less current for same voltage.
  • Capacitor (F) — Stores charge; blocks DC, passes AC.
  • Inductor (H) — Stores energy in magnetic field; opposes change in current.
  • Diode — Allows current in one direction only. Used in rectification (AC→DC).
  • Transistor — Semiconductor switch or amplifier.
  • Transformer — Changes AC voltage and current levels using mutual inductance. Only works with AC.
  • Fuse — Safety device that melts if current exceeds rated value. Must be correct rating — never fit higher value.
  • LED — Light Emitting Diode — emits light when forward biased.

AC and DC

  • DC (Direct Current) — flows in one direction only (e.g., batteries)
  • AC (Alternating Current) — reverses direction periodically (e.g., mains supply, radio signals)

UK mains electricity: 230V AC at 50Hz (Betts, 2019). Audio speech range: 300–3000Hz.

Conductors and Insulators

  • Conductors: All metals, water (on surface of insulators when wet)
  • Insulators: Plastic, rubber, wood, glass, ceramics — but may conduct on their surface when wet

Frequency and Wavelength

λ(m) = 300 / f(MHz)

Inverse: f(MHz) = 300 / λ(m)

FrequencyWavelength
1 MHz300m
3 MHz100m
10 MHz30m
30 MHz10m
100 MHz3m
300 MHz1m

Rule: Higher frequency = shorter wavelength.

Frequency Bands

AbbreviationNameRange
MFMedium Frequency0.3–3 MHz
HFHigh Frequency3–30 MHz
VHFVery High Frequency30–300 MHz
UHFUltra High Frequency300–3000 MHz

Decibels (dB)

Decibels express power ratios on a logarithmic scale:

dBPower Ratio
+3 dB× 2 (double)
+6 dB× 4
+10 dB× 10
−3 dB× 0.5 (half)
−10 dB× 0.1 (one-tenth)

Study Tips

You MUST know Ohm's Law (V=IR) and the power formula (P=VI) for the exam. Practice quick calculations. Remember: +3dB = double power, +10dB = ten times power. Know the wavelength formula λ = 300/f(MHz). Know that capacitors in series/parallel are the opposite of resistors.

References

  • Betts, A. (2019) Foundation Licence Now! 5th edn. Bedford: RSGB, pp. 27–56.
  • RSGB (2024) Foundation Exam Syllabus: Technical Basics. Available at: https://rsgb.org/main/clubs-and-education/for-students/ (Accessed: 15 March 2026).

title: Transmitters and Receivers
description: How radio transmitters and receivers work: oscillators, modulators, amplifiers, detectors, and modulation types (AM, FM, SSB, CW).
content:
The Transmitter

A radio transmitter converts information (voice, data, Morse code) into radio frequency signals. The basic building blocks are:

  1. Audio stage — Amplifies the weak microphone signal
  2. Modulator — Combines audio signal with carrier to produce modulated RF
  3. Frequency generator (oscillator) — Generates the carrier frequency. Must be accurate to avoid transmitting off-band.
  4. RF power amplifier — Amplifies the modulated signal to the required transmission power

Modulation Types

ModeHow It WorksEMC RiskNotes
AMAmplitude of carrier varies with audio; constant frequencyHigh — level varies with speechOver-modulation causes splatter on adjacent channels
FMFrequency of carrier varies with audio; constant amplitudeLow — constant amplitude outputOver-modulation causes interference to neighbours
SSBOnly one sideband transmitted; USB above 10MHz, LSB belowHighest — varies continuouslyMost power-efficient voice mode for HF (Betts, 2019)
CWCarrier switched on/off in Morse code patternsModerateNarrowest bandwidth mode
DataDigital modes (RTTY, PSK31, FT8 etc)Low for constant-level modesMany have constant power output

The Receiver

A radio receiver extracts information from incoming radio signals. The basic blocks are:

  1. Tuning and RF amplifier — Selects the wanted signal from all signals received by the antenna and amplifies it
  2. Detector (demodulator) — Extracts the original audio from the modulated signal. The mode switch must match the TX modulation type.
  3. Audio amplifier — Amplifies the audio signal to drive the loudspeaker or headphones
  4. Loudspeaker — Converts audio electrical signal to sound

Key Receiver Controls

ControlFunction
TuningSets transmit and receive frequency
Volume / AF gainSets loudspeaker volume
Squelch / MutingSilences audio when no signal present. Adjust to just suppress background noise.
Mode switchSelects AM, FM, USB, LSB, CW. Must match transmitter mode.
RITReceiver Incremental Tuning — offsets receive from transmit frequency. Used on HF SSB to fine-tune without changing TX frequency.
Repeater offsetSets TX frequency offset: −600kHz (2m) or +1.6MHz (70cm)
Tone burst / CTCSSActivates repeater. ON for repeater, OFF for simplex.
Microphone gainSets audio input level. Too high causes over-modulation.
Power high/lowSelects transmit power level

Study Tips

Know the transmitter and receiver block diagrams and what each stage does. Understand the difference between AM, FM, and SSB — SSB is most efficient for HF voice, FM is used on VHF/UHF. Know what RIT does and when to use it. Remember: mode switch on receiver must match the transmitter's mode.

References

  • Betts, A. (2019) Foundation Licence Now! 5th edn. Bedford: RSGB, pp. 57–78.
  • RSGB (2024) Foundation Exam Syllabus: Transmitters and Receivers. Available at: https://rsgb.org/main/clubs-and-education/for-students/ (Accessed: 15 March 2026).

title: Feeders and Antennas
description: Coaxial cable, connectors, antenna types (dipole, ground plane, Yagi, end-fed), polarisation, baluns, ATU, SWR, and dummy loads.
content:
Coaxial Cable (Feeder)

A feeder connects your transceiver to the antenna. The most common type is coaxial cable with a central conductor carrying the signal surrounded by a braided outer screen. The screen confines RF to the cable.

Connectors

  • BNC — Smaller connector, used on test equipment and some VHF radios
  • PL259 — Larger UHF connector, common on HF equipment; mates with SO239 socket

The screen must be properly connected to the plug body to form a continuous shield.

Common Antenna Types

AntennaLengthPatternBalun?Notes
Half-wave dipole (½λ)½ wavelength total (two ¼λ arms)Bidirectional — radiates from sides, poorly off endsYesBasic antenna; foundation for all others
Quarter-wave ground plane (¼λ)¼ wavelength element + 4 radialsOmnidirectional — does not radiate verticallyNoRadials form artificial ground plane acting as RF mirror
YagiDriven element = ½λ dipole + directors + reflectorDirectional — maximum toward tapering (director) endYesGain focused in one direction; used for DX and TV antennas
5/8-wave ground plane5/8 wavelength elementOmnidirectional; better toward horizon than ¼λNoCoil at base for matching. Most practical at VHF/UHF.
End-fed wireWhatever length availableVariableATU neededEasy at HF. High EMC risk at feed end — best fed from far end of garden.

Polarisation

  • Rule: TX and RX antennas must use the same polarisation (Betts, 2019)
  • VHF/UHF FM convention: Vertical
  • VHF/UHF SSB convention: Horizontal
  • Mobile antennas: Always vertical (practical reasons)

ERP (Effective Radiated Power)

ERP = antenna gain × transmit power

Antenna Tuning Unit (ATU)

Matches a mismatched antenna to the transmitter. Fitted in the feeder, usually at the transmitter end. Needed when antenna is not the correct size for the operating frequency — common for HF multi-band operation.

SWR Meter

Measures forward and reflected power in the feeder to determine match quality.

  • Ideal SWR: 1:1
  • High SWR causes: Antenna wrong length, antenna damaged, feeder fault, wrong frequency
  • Action on high SWR: Investigate cause before continuing to transmit

Balun (Balanced-to-Unbalanced)

Converts single-ended coaxial feed to balanced two-wire feed required by a dipole. Fitted at the junction of coaxial cable and dipole antenna. Without it, RF flows back down the coax screen into the shack, causing interference.

Dummy Load

A precision resistor absorbing full transmitter output power without radiating. Well screened. Used for testing and adjusting transmitter without going on air.

Study Tips

Know the five antenna types and their radiation patterns. Remember: balun needed for dipoles and Yagis, ATU needed for end-fed wires. Understand SWR (1:1 is perfect). Know VHF FM = vertical polarisation, SSB = horizontal. Know what a dummy load is for.

References

  • Betts, A. (2019) Foundation Licence Now! 5th edn. Bedford: RSGB, pp. 79–98.
  • RSGB (2024) UK Band Plans. Available at: https://rsgb.org/main/operating/band-plans/ (Accessed: 15 March 2026).

title: Propagation
description: How radio waves travel: ground wave, sky wave, ionosphere layers (D/E/F), line of sight, MUF, and factors affecting range.
content:
How Radio Waves Travel

Radio waves can travel from transmitter to receiver by several different paths, depending on the frequency and conditions.

Propagation Modes

ModeFrequenciesRangeMechanism
Ground waveMF and lower HFShort to medium (tens to a few hundred km)Wave follows earth's curvature
Sky wave (ionospheric)HF (3–30 MHz)Up to 4000km per hop; worldwide with multiple hopsRefracted back to earth by ionosphere
Line of sightVHF and UHF10–80km depending on terrain and antenna heightDirect path between antennas

The Ionosphere

The ionosphere (70–400km altitude) is created by UV radiation from the sun ionising upper atmosphere gases (Betts, 2019). It has three main layers:

LayerHeightPresentEffect
D layerLowestDaytime onlyAbsorbs/attenuates lower HF
E layerMiddleMainly daytimeReflects MF and lower HF
F layerHighest (70–400km)Day and night (splits into F1/F2 during day)Long-distance HF DX propagation

Ionisation strength varies with time of day (sunlight) and season.

Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF)

The highest frequency that will be refracted back to earth at a given time.

  • Daytime: Up to 30 MHz or more
  • Night: Can drop to ~3 MHz
  • Strategy: Choose operating frequency slightly below MUF

A single hop can reach up to 4000km. Worldwide communication is possible with multiple hops.

Buildings and Radio Waves

  • HF: Penetrates buildings relatively easily — wavelength large compared to building
  • VHF/UHF: Buildings are a significant obstacle. A window smaller than the wavelength acts as a useful aperture.

Factors Affecting Range

  • Transmitter power — Doubling power does NOT double range (inverse square law)
  • Antenna height — Higher is better for VHF/UHF
  • Antenna gain — A Yagi focuses power in the wanted direction
  • Frequency — Higher frequency = more obstruction from buildings and terrain
  • Terrain — Hills cause shadows; curvature of earth limits line-of-sight

Study Tips

Know the three propagation modes and which frequencies use each. Remember: D layer absorbs, F layer refracts for long-distance. The D layer disappears at night, improving HF propagation on lower bands. Know what MUF means and that you should operate just below it. VHF/UHF is line-of-sight — antenna height matters most.

References

  • Betts, A. (2019) Foundation Licence Now! 5th edn. Bedford: RSGB, pp. 99–112.
  • RSGB (2024) Foundation Exam Syllabus: Propagation. Available at: https://rsgb.org/main/clubs-and-education/for-students/ (Accessed: 15 March 2026).

title: EMC (Electromagnetic Compatibility)
description: Understanding interference paths, causes and cures, ferrite filters, RF earth, EMC best practices, and dealing with neighbours.
content:
What is EMC?

Electromagnetic Compatibility (EMC) is the avoidance of interference between electronic equipment. As a radio amateur, your transmitter can potentially cause interference to nearby electronic devices (Betts, 2019), and you must know how to prevent and resolve this.

Interference Paths

RF energy from your transmitter can enter affected equipment via several paths:

  • Path A: Pickup on mains power lead
  • Path B: Pickup on individual power leads
  • Paths C/D: Pickup on loudspeaker leads
  • Path E: Direct pickup in electronics
  • Path F: Pickup on FM tuner antenna lead

Causes and Cures

CauseCure
Direct pickup — field strength too highMove antenna further from house. Mount antenna high above other wiring.
RF conducted along mains cablesFit ferrite ring filters on all power leads (mains and DC).
RF from antenna picked up by wires into affected deviceMove antenna away. Fit filters on leads entering affected device.
RF fed back into mains earth wiresFit separate RF earth (metal spike near shack).

Ferrite Filters

A magnetic core ring around which cable is wound to block RF. Recommended: ~20 turns, or 4 rings × 5 turns. Clip-on ferrites are available for cables with moulded plugs — no need to cut wires or open equipment.

RF Earth

A metal spike driven into the ground close to the shack, connected directly to the transmitter or feeder entry. Provides RF return path without using mains earth wiring. Warning: Must consult an electrician before fitting if your property has a PME supply.

EMC Risk by Mode (Best to Worst)

  1. FM — constant amplitude, lowest risk
  2. Data modes (constant level)
  3. CW
  4. AM
  5. SSB — level varies continuously, highest risk

Best Practices

  • Use a balanced dipole antenna with balun — minimises RF on feeder
  • Feed end-fed antenna from the far end of the garden, not the house end
  • Lower transmit power reduces likelihood of interference
  • Do NOT fit home-made filters in mains — unsafe at Foundation level
  • Stop transmitting immediately if a neighbour complains; resolve before resuming

Dealing with Neighbours

  • Approach: Be co-operative — ask to see the problem and carry out tests
  • If not resolved: Contact RSGB EMC committee or Ofcom for independent assistance
  • Ofcom's role: May inspect both stations; likely to ask both parties to keep interference logs

Study Tips

Know the interference paths and their cures. Remember ferrite filters (~20 turns or 4×5). Know the EMC risk order (FM=best, SSB=worst). Understand that you should stop transmitting if a neighbour complains and work cooperatively to resolve the issue.

References

  • Betts, A. (2019) Foundation Licence Now! 5th edn. Bedford: RSGB, pp. 113–128.
  • Ofcom (2024) Amateur Radio Licence Terms, Conditions and Limitations. Available at: https://www.ofcom.org.uk/manage-your-licence/radiocommunication-licences/amateur-radio (Accessed: 15 March 2026).

title: Operating Practices and Procedures
description: Phonetic alphabet, Q-codes, RST signal reports, calling procedures, repeaters, CTCSS, tone burst, log keeping, and operating etiquette.
content:
The Phonetic Alphabet

The NATO/ICAO phonetic alphabet is used to spell out callsigns clearly (Betts, 2019):

ABCDEFGHI
AlphaBravoCharlieDeltaEchoFoxtrotGolfHotelIndia
JKLMNOPQR
JulietKiloLimaMikeNovemberOscarPapaQuebecRomeo
STUVWXYZ
SierraTangoUniformVictorWhiskyX-rayYankeeZulu

Q-Codes

CodeMeaning
QRGExact frequency
QRMMan-made interference
QRNNatural interference (static)
QROIncrease transmitter power
QRPDecrease power / low power operation
QRSSend more slowly
QRTStop transmitting / close station
QRXWait / standby
QRZWho is calling me?
QSBSignal strength varying (fading)
QSLI confirm receipt / QSL card
QSOCommunication with another station
QSYChange frequency
QTHMy location / address

RST Signal Reporting

  • R — Readability (1-5): 1 = Unreadable → 5 = Totally readable
  • S — Strength (1-9): 1 = Faint → 9 = Very strong
  • T — Tone (1-9): CW only. 1 = Extremely rough → 9 = Pure DC note

A typical SSB report is 59. A typical CW report is 599.

Calling Procedure

Before Calling

  1. Listen on the frequency
  2. Ask "Is the frequency in use?" — wait
  3. Proceed only if clear

VHF FM CQ Call

"CQ CQ CQ this is M6ABC calling CQ"

HF SSB CQ Call

"CQ CQ CQ CQ CQ CQ this is M6ABC M6ABC calling CQ CQ CQ M6ABC calling CQ"

Repeat multiple times on HF to allow listeners to tune in accurately. Do not adjust main TX frequency if replying station is off-tune — use RIT. Move off calling channel to a working frequency after making contact.

Calling Channels

  • 2m FM: 145.500 MHz
  • 2m SSB: 144.300 MHz
  • 70cm FM: 433.500 MHz

Repeaters

  1. Tune to repeater output frequency
  2. Select repeater offset: −600kHz (2m) or +1.6MHz (70cm)
  3. Enable tone burst (1750Hz) and/or CTCSS as required
  4. Press PTT and call: "M6ABC listening through"

CTCSS

Continuous Tone Coded Squelch System: a sub-audible tone (70–250Hz) transmitted continuously to open the repeater. Prevents accidental access to adjacent repeaters. Tones are filtered out before the loudspeaker.

Tone Burst

1750Hz tone held for ~0.5 seconds to activate older-style repeaters.

Station Log

Keeping a log is recommended but not legally required. Useful for: reference, required by Ofcom during interference investigation, needed for QSL cards and contest entries. Record: Date, Time (UTC), Frequency, Mode, Power, Station worked, Signal reports sent/received, Remarks.

Etiquette

  • Anyone may be listening — always be polite and respectful
  • No abuse, bad language, or deliberate interference
  • If subjected to abuse, do not respond — find another frequency
  • Q-codes are most useful on Morse or with non-English speakers
  • Report persistent abuse to RSGB AROS (confidential)

Study Tips

Learn the phonetic alphabet and key Q-codes (QRM, QRN, QRZ, QTH, QSL, QSY). Know the RST system (59 for SSB, 599 for CW). Know calling frequencies (145.500 for 2m FM). Understand repeater offsets (−600kHz on 2m, +1.6MHz on 70cm) and what CTCSS does.

References

  • Betts, A. (2019) Foundation Licence Now! 5th edn. Bedford: RSGB, pp. 129–154.
  • RSGB (2024) UK Band Plans. Available at: https://rsgb.org/main/operating/band-plans/ (Accessed: 15 March 2026).

title: Safety
description: Electrical safety, mains wiring, RF burns, antenna safety, car battery hazards, headphone risks, and first aid for electric shock.
content:
High Voltage — Mains Electricity

UK mains is 230V AC (Betts, 2019) — potentially lethal.

  • Never work on live mains equipment
  • Switch off and unplug before any internal work
  • Fit correct fuse rating — never substitute a higher value
  • Do not take lids off mains-powered equipment at Foundation level

Mains Plug Wiring

Wire ColourConnection
BrownLive (L)
BlueNeutral (N)
Yellow/GreenEarth (E)
  • Flex held captive by cord grip
  • Insulation continues close up to the pin
  • No frays or whiskers
  • All strands secured
  • Correct fuse rating (3A for most small appliances)

High Current Hazards

  • Can overheat wires and start fires even at low voltage
  • Remove rings and metallic wristwatches when working with high-current sources
  • Short circuits from car batteries can cause red-hot wires

Accidents — Electric Shock First Aid

  1. Cut off the power before touching a casualty — do NOT touch them while they are in contact with the source
  2. Summon adult help
  3. Anyone who has suffered shock must receive medical attention

RF Burns

Deep tissue burns from touching antenna or feeder elements carrying RF. May not be initially painful; full extent not apparent until later. Never touch antenna during transmission. Insulated but unscreened wires can also cause burns.

Antenna Safety

  • Mount clear of overhead power lines — extremely dangerous
  • Secure mounting — wind loading can be very high
  • Consider lightning risk for tall antennas
  • Antenna erection always supervised — never climb alone
  • People on ground must wear hard hats
  • Planning permission may be required for large masts
  • Disconnect and earth during lightning storms

PME (Protective Multiple Earthing)

Connecting an RF earth to a PME supply can cause dangerous currents. Always consult a qualified electrician before fitting an RF earth.

Car Batteries

  • Risks: Very high short-circuit current, hydrogen gas during charging (explosive), corrosive acid
  • Do not charge indoors
  • Spill on skin: immerse in running water for 15 minutes
  • Spill in eye: immediate and constant irrigation then medical attention

Headphones

  • Hearing risk: Permanent hearing damage from excessive volume — may take a year to become apparent
  • Volume rule: Turn down until too quiet, then slightly up — not up until it feels too loud
  • Electrical risk: May complete electrical circuit during servicing — do not wear when working on live equipment

Other Hazards

  • Sharp tools — cuts
  • Soldering irons — burns
  • Trailing wires — trip hazard; can drag equipment exposing live parts
  • Mains wires under carpets — become frayed unnoticed; fire and shock risk

Study Tips

Safety questions are common in the exam. Know: first aid for electric shock (cut off power first, never touch casualty). Know mains plug colours (Brown=Live, Blue=Neutral, Yellow-Green=Earth). Know that antennas near power lines are extremely dangerous. Know RF burns can be deep and delayed. Know the headphone volume rule.

References

  • Betts, A. (2019) Foundation Licence Now! 5th edn. Bedford: RSGB, pp. 155–170.
  • Health and Safety Executive (2024) Electrical Safety at Work. Available at: https://www.hse.gov.uk/electricity/ (Accessed: 15 March 2026).
